title: How pieces see, attack and defend
blurb: Learn what every piece can attack, spot pieces nobody is guarding, and master the four ways to answer an attack.
deeperTitle: True piece value vs points; finding loose pieces

core.title: Every piece has a line of sight
body: A piece **attacks** a square when it could capture something standing there. Bishops, rooks, queens and knights attack the squares they can move to.
**Pawns are the odd ones out.** They move straight ahead, but they attack diagonally.
This bishop sits in the middle of an empty board and attacks **13 squares**.

board.caption: The highlighted squares are the ones the bishop attacks.

core.prompt: How many squares does this rook attack?
core.explain: Seven along its file and seven along its rank. A rook on an empty board always attacks **14** squares, wherever it stands.

core.prompt: White's pawn on e4 can capture one black piece. Tap it.
core.explain: The pawn attacks **diagonally**, so it takes the knight on d5. The rook straight ahead on e5 is safe from it.

core.title: Defended, or loose?
body: A piece is **defended** when a friendly piece could take back after a capture. A piece that nobody defends is **loose**.
A loose piece that is also attacked is **hanging**. That is a free gift, so check yours and your opponent's before every move.

core.prompt: White to move. Tap the black piece that nobody defends.
core.explain: The d7 pawn guards the knight, the bishop guards the d7 pawn, and the king guards the other pawns. But **nobody guards the bishop on f5**, so the queen can simply take it.

core.title: Four ways to answer an attack
body: When one of your pieces is attacked, you have four answers:
**Defend** it, so that a capture would cost your opponent more than it wins.
Knights jump over pieces, so you can never block a knight. Let us practise each one.

core.prompt: Black's pawn attacks your queen. Answer by **moving** her to safety.
core.hint: Do not take the e5 pawn: the d6 pawn would take your queen.
core.explain: Any safe square works. A move with a capture, like **Qxd6**, is even better, because nothing guards that pawn.

core.prompt: Their bishop attacks your knight, and nothing protects it. Answer by **capturing** the attacker.
core.hint: Which of your pieces can take the bishop on g4?
core.explain: **hxg4**. The pawn takes the bishop and nothing takes back. Pawns are excellent at removing attackers.

core.prompt: Their rook attacks your queen, and the rook is guarded. Answer by **blocking**.
core.hint: Which piece can step onto the e-file between the two of them?
core.explain: **Be3** steps between the rook and the queen. The queen protects the bishop, so the rook cannot take it for free.

core.prompt: Their bishop attacks your e4 pawn. Answer by **defending** it.
core.hint: Which of your pieces could take back on e4?
core.explain: Any move that guards e4 works. If the bishop now takes the pawn, you take the bishop back and win a piece for a pawn.

core.prompt: Which of these is NOT a way to answer an attack?
core.explain: The four answers are: **move**, **capture**, **block** and **defend**. Ignoring the attack is how pieces get lost.

core.prompt: Their knight attacks your bishop on d3. Save it any way you like.
core.hint: You cannot block a knight, but you have other answers.
core.explain: Moving the bishop works, and so does taking the knight with **Bxf4**. A good player checks all four answers before choosing.

core.title: Free pieces
core.intro: Each of these has a piece nobody is guarding. Take it.

puzzles.hint: Look for the piece with no defender.
puzzles.explain: The knight on d5 had no defender, so the rook wins it for free.
The knight on c3 was unprotected. Always check before you leave a piece out on its own.

puzzles.hint: The queen is loose. Does taking her do more than win material?
puzzles.explain: The queen was undefended, and taking her with check was also checkmate. Loose pieces cost games.

deeper.title: Points are a guide, not a law
body: Chess players count material in points: **pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9**. The king has no value because he can never be traded.
Use the points to compare trades. But a piece is worth what it does. A knight that wins the game is worth far more than 3, and a bishop stuck behind its own pawns is worth less.

deeper.prompt: You trade your bishop for your opponent's rook. How is that for you?
options: Good: you win 2 points (rook 5 against bishop 3)
Even: all pieces are the same
deeper.explain: A rook for a minor piece is called **winning the exchange**. You come out two points ahead.

deeper.prompt: Which of these trades is fair?
deeper.explain: Knight and bishop are both worth 3. A queen (9) for a rook and a pawn (6) loses 3 points, and a rook (5) for two pawns (2) loses 3 points.

deeper.prompt: Your knight is attacked by a pawn, and your rook defends the knight. Is the knight safe?
options: No: the pawn takes the knight, and you only win a pawn back
deeper.explain: Being defended is not enough. The pawn is worth 1 and the knight is worth 3, so after the trade you are **2 points down**. Move the knight.
Each piece guards another in a chain: the bishop guards b7, the rook guards the bishop. But **nobody guards the rook**. Look at the end of every chain.

deeper.prompt: Black to move. Tap the white piece that nobody defends.
deeper.explain: The knight is guarded by the b2 pawn, the pawn by the bishop, the bishop by the queen, and the queen by the rook. The bishop on c4 stands alone.

deeper.prompt: White to move. Win something for free, but check what is defended first.
deeper.hint: One black piece has no defender.
deeper.explain: **Qxd5** wins the knight. The tempting **Qxh7+** loses the queen, because the king takes it. Always ask who defends the target.

deeper.title: Loose pieces drop off
deeper.intro: A little harder: the loose piece is not always the obvious one.

puzzles.hint: The bishop sees all the way down the diagonal.
puzzles.explain: Nothing guards the knight, so the long diagonal wins it.

puzzles.hint: A knight attacks in an L shape.
puzzles.explain: The bishop stood alone on d4, and the knight takes it.

puzzles.hint: The rook has no defender, and the queen sees it along the file.
puzzles.explain: The rook was loose, and the capture even comes with check.

deeper.prompt: What is the best habit to build?
options: Before every move, check which pieces are loose, mine and theirs
Count how many pawns are left
Only move the piece you moved last
deeper.explain: Most games below 1200 are decided by a piece that someone left unguarded. This one habit wins more games than any opening.
